content: Vitamin D deficiency is frequently observed in individuals with chronic liver diseases. Enhancing vitamin D levels may potentially provide health benefits for these patients. This study aimed to evaluate both the positive and negative effects of vitamin D supplementation in adults suffering from chronic liver diseases. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group Controlled Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and others, up to November 2020. They also reviewed bibliographies of relevant studies and consulted experts and pharmaceutical companies to identify additional trials. The inclusion criteria were randomized clinical trials comparing vitamin D supplementation, in any dose, duration, or route of administration, against placebo or no intervention in adults with chronic liver diseases. Vitamin D could be administered as vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol), vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol), or active forms such as alfacalcidol, calcidiol, or calcitriol. The review included 27 randomized clinical trials involving 1,979 adult participants. Of these, 12 trials with 945 participants were newly added in this update. All trials were assessed to have a high risk of bias and followed a parallel-group design. Eleven trials were conducted in high-income countries, while 16 were conducted in middle-income countries. The participants included individuals with chronic hepatitis C (10 trials), liver cirrhosis (5 trials), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (11 trials), and liver transplant recipients (1 trial). Baseline vitamin D levels were reported in all trials, with nine trials including participants with adequate vitamin D levels (≥20 ng/mL) and 18 trials including participants with insufficient levels (<20 ng/mL). Vitamin D was administered orally in 24 trials, intramuscularly in two trials, and both orally and intramuscularly in one trial. The average duration of supplementation was six months, with a mean follow-up period of seven months. Twenty trials tested vitamin D3 (1,592 participants; 44% women; mean age 48 years), three trials tested vitamin D2 (156 participants; 28% women; mean age 54 years), four trials tested calcitriol (291 participants; 60% women; mean age 52 years), and one trial tested calcidiol (18 participants; 0% women; mean age 52 years). One trial did not specify the form of vitamin D used. Twelve trials employed a placebo, while the remaining 15 trials used no intervention in the control group. Fourteen trials appeared to be free of vested interests, while 11 trials did not disclose information on funding or sponsorship. Two trials were funded by industry. The evidence regarding the effects of vitamin D supplementation compared to placebo or no intervention on all-cause mortality was highly uncertain (risk ratio [RR] 0.86, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.51 to 1.45; 27 trials; 1,979 participants). The mean follow-up period was seven months, ranging from one to 18 months. Similarly, the evidence on liver-related mortality was very uncertain (RR 1.62, 95% CI 0.08 to 34.66; 1 trial; 18 participants; 12-month follow-up). The data on serious adverse events, such as hypercalcemia (RR 5.00, 95% CI 0.25 to 100.8; 1 trial; 76 participants), myocardial infarction (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.08 to 6.81; 2 trials; 86 participants), thyroiditis (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.01 to 7.91; 1 trial; 68 participants), circular hemorrhoidal prolapse (RR 3.00, 95% CI 0.14 to 65.9; 1 trial; 20 participants), and bronchopneumonia (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.02 to 7.32; 1 trial; 20 participants), was also highly uncertain. Non-serious adverse events were similarly uncertain. The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was rated as very low. No data were available on liver-related morbidity, such as gastrointestinal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, ascites, or liver cancer. Additionally, there were no data on health-related quality of life. The evidence was also very uncertain regarding the effects of vitamin D supplementation on virological responses in individuals with chronic hepatitis C. In conclusion, due to the high risk of bias, insufficient statistical power of the included trials, and the very low certainty of the evidence, it remains unclear whether vitamin D supplementation increases or decreases all-cause mortality, liver-related mortality, serious adverse events, or non-serious adverse events in adults with chronic liver diseases. There is a significant lack of data on liver-related morbidity and health-related quality of life. Further research focusing on clinically important outcomes is urgently needed.
